question: Along with the Hun invasions, which ruler of Malwa contributed to the downfall of Gupta power?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Yashodharman.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Yashodharman of Malwa rose in the sixth century and, along with the Hun invasions, brought down the remaining Gupta power (यशोधर्मन — मालवा का शासक, गुप्त पतन में योगदान)

 

• His rise shows how powerful regional rulers cut away from the Gupta centre as the dynasty weakened.

 

• Yashodharman is remembered for defeating the Hun king Mihirakula, so he also checked the Huns.

 

• The last Gupta ruler named in the notes is Vishnugupta, and the dynasty's end came about 550 AD.

 

• After this decline, north India broke into many kingdoms until the rise of Harshavardhana.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Yashodharman's victory pillar is known from Mandasor inscriptions.

 

• The empire shrank to its Bengal and Magadha core in the sixth century.

 

• The rise of feudal lords was a parallel factor in the end.

 

• The Mandasor inscription of Yashodharman claims victories in regions that neither the Guptas nor the Huns could control.

 

• After the collapse, north India came to be ruled by regional houses such as the Maukharis and Pushyabhutis.

 

NOTE

 

• Prabhakaravardhana (Option 2): Prabhakaravardhana ruled at Thanesar as the father of Harshavardhana and lived after the Gupta decline had set in. He belonged to Pushyabhuti, not Malwa.

 

• Isanavarman (Option 3): Isanavarman was a Maukhari ruler of Kannauj in the sixth century and a rival of the later Guptas. He was not a king of Malwa.

 

• Harshavardhana (Option 4): Harshavardhana ruled in the seventh century, long after the end of Gupta power, and was a king of Thanesar and Kannauj. He cannot have helped cause the Gupta fall.

question: Who was the last ruler of the Gupta dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vishnugupta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vishnugupta was the last ruler of the Gupta dynasty; under him the dynasty fell because of the Hun invasions, the rise of feudal lords and the rise of Yashodharman of Malwa (विष्णुगुप्त — अंतिम गुप्त शासक)

 

• By his time the empire had shrunk to a small kingdom, and real power rested with regional kings.

 

• The dynasty's rule is dated from about 320 AD to about 550 AD in the notes' scheme.

 

• Skandagupta was the last great ruler, but the end of the family came with Vishnugupta.

 

• His reign is a convenient marker for the end of the Classical Age in north India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Gupta line is one of the longest in early Indian history.

 

• After the Guptas, the Maukharis, Later Guptas and Pushyabhutis emerged.

 

• Harshavardhana later united much of the north.

 

• The later Guptas of Magadha formed a separate line and should not be confused with the imperial Guptas.

 

• Even in its last years the family kept control over parts of Bengal and Magadha for some time.

 

NOTE

 

• Skandagupta (Option 1): Skandagupta was the last great ruler, but several weaker kings followed him. He is not the final ruler, though students often confuse the two labels.

 

• Budhagupta (Option 2): Budhagupta was a later king who ruled after Skandagupta and is known from inscriptions, but he was not the last ruler. At least one more king followed him.

 

• Narasimhagupta (Option 3): Narasimhagupta Baladitya ruled in the late period and is remembered for patronising Nalanda and resisting the Huns. He was not the final ruler named in the dynasty's list.

question:
Match the Gupta administrative units in Column I with their heads in Column II.

Column I: a. Bhukti   b. Vishaya   c. Vithi   d. Grama

Column II: i. Gramika   ii. Vishayapati   iii. Uparika   iv. Vithimahattara
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is Bhukti - Uparika, Vishaya - Vishayapati, Vithi - Vithimahattara and Grama - Gramika (गुप्त प्रशासनिक इकाइयाँ — भुक्ति, विषय, वीथी, ग्राम)

 

• The Bhukti was the largest division or province, governed by the Uparika.

 

• The Vishaya was the district, under the Vishayapati, and below it the Vithi (sub-district) was led by the Vithimahattara.

 

• The Grama (village) was the smallest unit of administration and was headed by the Gramika.

 

• The structure runs from top to bottom: empire, Bhukti, Vishaya, Vithi and Grama.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kumaramatyas and Ayuktas kept the king in touch with provincial administration.

 

• The Bhukti was the largest administrative division, comparable to a modern state or province.

 

• The village headman collected local revenue.

 

• Copper plates from Bengal show that the Vishaya was run with a board including a town banker, caravan leader and chief scribe.

 

• The Uparika was appointed directly by the king and ruled the Bhukti, which could be compared with a modern province.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 2): This key assigns Vishayapati to Bhukti and Uparika to Vishaya and then pairs Vithi with Gramika, so it swaps the top levels and the bottom levels. The Uparika headed the province and the Gramika the village.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i (Option 3): This key correctly places Bhukti-Uparika and Vishaya-Vishayapati but puts Vithimahattara at the village and Gramika at the sub-district. The Gramika led the village, not the Vithi.

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv (Option 4): This key puts the Gramika at the Bhukti level, the Uparika at the Vithi and the Vithimahattara at the Grama. The village headman cannot head the largest division, so the order is inverted.

question: In the Gupta administration, the Sarthavaha was the
solution_text:
The correct answer is leader of merchants and caravans.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Sarthavaha was the leader of merchants and caravans, an important figure in Gupta trade and guild life (सार्थवाह — व्यापारियों और कारवाँ का नेता)

 

• He guided caravans over long routes, linking towns and ports and bringing goods from far regions.

 

• Such leaders were influential in the economy of the Gupta age, where trade flourished through gold Dinara coinage.

 

• The title is often confused with offices of the state such as the Sandhivigrahika or the Dandapasika, but the Sarthavaha was commercial rather than official.

 

• Caravan leaders could also be head of trading guilds in many sources.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sarthavaha literally means leader of a sartha or caravan.

 

• Trade by sea flourished from the western ports of the Gupta empire.

 

• Guilds of merchants and artisans were a feature of urban administration.

 

• Gupta trade used overland routes to Central Asia and sea routes from ports such as Tamralipti and Bharuch.

 

• Merchant guilds had a voice in local administration and banking, so trade leaders were influential.

 

NOTE

 

• officer for war and peace (Option 1): The officer for war and peace was the Sandhivigrahika, a minister handling diplomatic affairs and foreign relations. He was a state official, whereas the Sarthavaha was a leader of merchants.

 

• village headman (Option 2): The village headman was the Gramika, who headed the village, the smallest administrative unit. He was a rural functionary, not a trade leader.

 

• police and law-and-order officer (Option 3): The police and law-and-order officer was the Dandapasika, who kept order within the kingdom. He was a state servant and had nothing to do with leading merchant caravans.

question: In the Gupta administration, which officer served as the notary and keeper of records?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pustapala.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Pustapala was the notary and keeper of records in the Gupta administration, maintaining documents and registers (पुस्तपाल — अभिलेखपाल और लेखा-रक्षक)

 

• Such record-keepers were needed because the Guptas issued land grants and inscribed copper plates which had to be registered.

 

• Gupta administration was more decentralised than the Mauryan, but it still relied on trained scribes and officials in the districts.

 

• The Dhruvadhikaranika was linked with revenue or the treasury, and the Mahabaladhikrita with the army.

 

• The Dandapasika was the police officer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pustapala is also connected with land records in the later copper-plate grants.

 

• Mahadandanayaka was a high official of judicial and military functions.

 

• Written documents increased in importance as land grants became common.

 

• Land-grant copper plates to Brahmanas and religious institutions became common in the Gupta age, which increased the need for record keepers.

 

• Gupta land records show that officials had to maintain registers of fields, boundaries and donations.

 

NOTE

 

• Dandapasika (Option 1): The Dandapasika was the police and law-and-order officer, concerned with crime and punishment. He did not maintain written records, so he is not the notary.

 

• Dhruvadhikaranika (Option 3): The Dhruvadhikaranika was the officer in charge of revenue collection or the treasury, which is a financial function. Record-keeping and notarial work was handled by another official.

 

• Mahabaladhikrita (Option 4): The Mahabaladhikrita was a military officer, commander of the armed forces. His duties were about defence and not clerical records.

question: In the Gupta administration, which officer dealt with matters of war and peace and foreign affairs?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sandhivigrahika.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Sandhivigrahika was the officer who handled war and peace and foreign affairs, a sort of foreign minister of the Gupta state (संधिविग्रहिक — युद्ध-शांति और विदेश मामलों का मंत्री)

 

• The word combines sandhi (peace or treaty) and vigraha (war), which makes the function clear.

 

• Such an officer was important in an empire that practised diplomacy through marriage alliances and negotiated with distant powers such as Sri Lanka.

 

• He worked beside the Mahabaladhikrita, who commanded the armed forces, and the Mahadandanayaka, who held judicial and military duties.

 

• Titles like Mahasandhivigrahika appear in Gupta inscriptions for the chief of this department.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Harisena, who composed the Allahabad prashasti, himself held the post of Sandhivigrahika under Samudragupta.

 

• Gupta administration used a hierarchy of Amatyas and Kumaramatyas.

 

• Foreign contacts included embassies from Sri Lanka and distant frontier kings.

 

• The Allahabad inscription records that Harisena himself held the posts of Sandhivigrahika, Kumaramatya and Mahadandanayaka under Samudragupta.

 

• Mahadandanayaka was a senior officer with judicial and military duties.

 

NOTE

 

• Dandapasika (Option 1): The Dandapasika was the police and law-and-order officer, dealing with crime inside the empire. He was not a diplomat and did not handle peace treaties.

 

• Pustapala (Option 2): The Pustapala was the notary and keeper of records, concerned with documents. His clerical work was unrelated to war and peace or foreign policy.

 

• Mahabaladhikrita (Option 3): The Mahabaladhikrita was the commander of the armed forces, a purely military post. He led the army in war, but decisions on treaties and diplomacy were handled by the Sandhivigrahika.

question:
Consider the following statements about Gupta officials.

1. The Dandapasika was the police or law-and-order officer.

2. The Mahabaladhikrita was a military officer and commander of the armed forces.

3. The Gramika was the head of the Vishaya (district).

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The police and army statements are right, while statement 3 is wrong because the Gramika headed the village, whereas the Vishayapati headed the district (गुप्त अधिकारी — दंडपाशिक, महाबलाधिकृत, ग्रामिक)

 

• The Dandapasika looked after police and law and order, a function essential to internal security.

 

• The Mahabaladhikrita commanded the military forces, making him the head of the Gupta army establishment.

 

• The Gramika managed the Grama, the smallest unit of administration, where he dealt with local affairs and revenue collection.

 

• Gupta administration therefore had officers at every level from the king down to the village.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Uparika governed a Bhukti, the largest division.

 

• The Vithimahattara led the Vithi, a sub-district.

 

• Kumaramatyas were high-ranking officers among the Amatyas.

 

• Dandapasika officers are named in many Gupta and Vakataka land-grant inscriptions among the officials who were told of a grant.

 

• The Vishayapati headed the district and often worked with a local advisory board.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Statements 2 and 3 together would accept the Gramika as a district head, which is wrong, and would drop the true statement about the Dandapasika. The Gramika was a village head.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Statements 1 and 3 accept the Gramika as a district head. Both the police officer statement and the district claim cannot be right together, because statement 3 is false and statement 2 is true.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three statements would include the Gramika as a district head, which is false. The district head was the Vishayapati, so the combination is impossible.

question: Through which class of officers did the Gupta king keep close contact with provincial administration?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kumaramatyas and Ayuktas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Gupta king kept in close touch with provincial administration through officers called Kumaramatyas and Ayuktas (कुमारामात्य और आयुक्त — प्रांतीय प्रशासन से राजा का संपर्क)

 

• The Kumaramatya was a high-ranking officer among the Amatyas, usually posted to supervise provinces and districts.

 

• These officers worked between the central court and local heads such as the Uparika and Vishayapati.

 

• The Gupta system was layered: Bhukti, Vishaya, Vithi and Grama, each with its own head.

 

• Kumaramatyas were later seen as a regular cadre of the Gupta bureaucracy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Kumaramatya post appears in many Gupta seals.

 

• Ayuktas are officers whose title also appears in other early Indian administrative records.

 

• Gupta provincial officers helped carry out the king's orders.

 

• Kumaramatyas appear in Gupta-age land grants of Bengal, where they acted at district headquarters.

 

• The Gupta bureaucracy was less rigidly centralised than the Mauryan one, which gave governors more freedom.

 

NOTE

 

• Sandhivigrahikas and Dandapasikas (Option 1): Sandhivigrahikas dealt with foreign affairs and war and peace, while Dandapasikas were police officers. Neither group served mainly as the link between the king and provinces.

 

• Pustapalas and Sarthavahas (Option 3): Pustapalas were record keepers and Sarthavahas were leaders of merchants and caravans. One group served in clerical roles and the other in trade, so neither kept the king in touch with provinces.

 

• Gramikas and Vithimahattaras (Option 4): Gramikas and Vithimahattaras were local heads of a village and a sub-district. They were part of the provincial structure and not the officers who connected the king to it.

question:
Match the Gupta fiscal terms in Column I with their meanings in Column II.

Column I: a. Bhaga   b. Hiranya   c. Vishti   d. Dasaparadha

Column II: i. Fines from ten offences   ii. Forced labour   iii. King's share of agricultural produce   iv. Tax paid in cash
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct match is Bhaga - king's share of produce, Hiranya - cash tax, Vishti - forced labour and Dasaparadha - fines from ten offences (गुप्त कर शब्दावली — भाग, हिरण्य, विष्टि, दशापराध)

 

• Bhaga was the share of agricultural produce paid to the king as land revenue, the main source of state income.

 

• Hiranya was a tax paid in cash rather than in kind, which shows the use of money in the Gupta economy.

 

• Vishti (also Vaishthika) was forced labour demanded by the state or its officials.

 

• Dasaparadha denoted the fines collected for ten kinds of offences.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bhoga meant supplies given to the king and officials, often in kind.

 

• Uparikara was an additional levy imposed on land or on certain people.

 

• Kara was a tax or tribute that could be imposed on subjects or on subordinate rulers.

 

• A strong revenue base through Bhaga allowed Gupta emperors to maintain a large army and issue many gold coins.

 

• Hiranya payments in coin show that money circulated in the Gupta economy.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i (Option 1): This key gives Hiranya the meaning of forced labour and Vishti the meaning of a cash tax, swapping the two. Hiranya (gold or cash) is the tax in money, and Vishti is compulsory labour.

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i (Option 2): This key assigns Bhaga to cash and Hiranya to the king's share. Bhaga was the share of produce and Hiranya the cash tax, so the first two pairs are interchanged.

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii (Option 3): This key makes Vishti the fines and Dasaparadha forced labour. Dasaparadha refers to fines for ten offences and Vishti to forced labour, so these two are exchanged.

question: Which Gupta-era fiscal term denotes dues that are 'to be surrendered' to the king or the state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Adeya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Adeya denotes dues or taxes that are 'to be surrendered' or given to the king or the state (अदेय — राज्य को देय बकाया कर)

 

• The Gupta tax system had many categories: Bhaga, Bhoga, Kara, Hiranya, Uparikara, Vishti, Dasaparadha and Adeya.

 

• Each term addressed a different kind of payment, whether in kind, in cash, in labour or as fines.

 

• The wide variety shows how organised the Gupta revenue system had become.

 

• The word itself conveys the meaning of something that is due and must be handed over.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bhoga was supplies provided to the king and officials.

 

• Kara could be paid by subjects or by subordinate rulers.

 

• Uparikara was an additional levy.

 

• Terms such as Bhoga and Adeya appear in copper-plate land grants that exempt donated villages from various dues.

 

• Taxes on trade and tolls were collected in addition to land revenue.

 

NOTE

 

• Bhaga (Option 1): Bhaga was the king's share of agricultural produce, collected as land revenue, a regular and basic tax. It does not carry the meaning of dues to be surrendered.

 

• Vishti (Option 2): Vishti was forced labour, also called Vaishthika, demanded from villagers by state officials. It is a labour obligation and not a general due to be handed over.

 

• Dasaparadha (Option 4): Dasaparadha referred to fines collected for ten offences. It was a judicial penalty and has no link with the sense of a due to be surrendered.

question:
Consider the following statements about Gupta taxation.

1. Bhoga meant supplies and provisions given to the king and officials, often in kind.

2. Hiranya was a tax paid in kind as a share of grain.

3. Vishti was forced labour demanded by the state or its officials.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The valid pair here is statements 1 and 3: Bhoga was supplies in kind for the king and officials and Vishti was forced labour, while statement 2 is wrong since Hiranya was a cash tax (गुप्तकालीन कर — भोग, हिरण्य, विष्टि)

 

• The contrast between Bhaga (grain share) and Hiranya (cash) is a regular exam point.

 

• Bhoga covered provisions such as food or goods supplied to officials during visits or to the court.

 

• Vishti or Vaishthika was compulsory service, a burden on villagers.

 

• The presence of cash taxes suggests the continued use of coins in Gupta trade.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Uparikara was an additional levy associated with land or special groups.

 

• Kara was a tax or tribute on subjects or subordinate rulers.

 

• Adeya was dues to be surrendered.

 

• Gupta land grants often exempt donated villages from burdens like Vishti, so the term appears in surviving records.

 

• Uparikara is another levy named among Gupta imposts, and it was imposed on certain lands or groups.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Statements 1 and 2 would accept Hiranya as a tax in kind, which is wrong. Hiranya was paid in cash, and this combination also drops the true statement on Vishti.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): Statements 2 and 3 include the false claim that Hiranya was paid in kind. It would also drop the true statement about Bhoga, so the combination is wrong.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three statements would include the false claim that Hiranya was paid in grain. Because statement 2 is false, the combination cannot be correct.

question: The Bhitargaon temple, the oldest surviving terracotta Hindu shrine with a roof and a high shikhara, is located in which district of Uttar Pradesh?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kanpur.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Bhitargaon temple is in the Kanpur district of Uttar Pradesh and is the oldest surviving terracotta Hindu shrine with a roof and a high shikhara, a fine example of Gupta architecture (भीतरगाँव मंदिर — कानपुर, उत्तर प्रदेश)

 

• The first temple-building activity in India began during the Gupta dynasty, and Bhitargaon is one of the best examples.

 

• The temple is made of brick and terracotta, with decorated panels, showing the skill of Gupta artisans.

 

• The Gupta age laid the foundation of later Nagara temple style.

 

• Its high shikhara foreshadows the tall spires of later north Indian temples.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Another early Gupta temple is the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh, in Lalitpur district.

 

• Bhitargaon is a village in the Kanpur Dehat area.

 

• Gupta temples began with simple flat-roofed shrines at Sanchi.

 

• Other early Gupta temples include the Vishnu temple at Tigawa near Jabalpur and the Parvati temple at Nachna Kuthara.

 

• Gupta temples often had a square sanctum with a flat roof, while Bhitargaon shows the high tower form.

 

NOTE

 

• Jhansi (Option 2): Jhansi district is in Bundelkhand and has Gupta-period remains in its region, but the Bhitargaon temple is not located there. The temple lies in a different district.

 

• Gwalior (Option 3): Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh is a different state and is not in Uttar Pradesh at all. The question already says the temple is in Uttar Pradesh, so Gwalior can be ruled out.

 

• Prayagraj (Option 4): Prayagraj (Allahabad) is known for the Allahabad pillar inscription of Samudragupta and is a major Gupta site, but the brick temple of Bhitargaon is not located in that district.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Ajanta caves.

1. The Ajanta caves are 29 rock-cut Buddhist caves in the Aurangabad region of Maharashtra.

2. The first phase belongs to the Satavahana period and to the Hinayana sect.

3. The second phase belongs to the Vakataka and Gupta period and to the Mahayana sect.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: Ajanta has 29 rock-cut Buddhist caves near Aurangabad, built in two phases, the first in the Satavahana period (Hinayana) and the second in the Vakataka-Gupta period (Mahayana) (अजंता गुफाएँ — दो चरण, हीनयान और महायान)

 

• In the Hinayana phase the Buddha was shown aniconically through symbols such as the stupa, wheel and footprints.

 

• In the Mahayana phase the Buddha was shown in human form, and images and murals multiplied.

 

• The Ajanta paintings are famous for their scenes from the Jataka stories and the life of the Buddha.

 

• The caves are rock-cut chaityas and viharas, serving as prayer halls and monasteries.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ajanta is in the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district of Maharashtra, earlier called Aurangabad.

 

• The caves were rediscovered by a British officer in 1819.

 

• Ellora caves nearby include Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves.

 

• Caves 9, 10, 12 and 13 of Ajanta belong to the earlier Hinayana phase, while Caves 1, 2, 16, 17 and 19 are of the later phase.

 

• Ajanta lies in the horseshoe-shaped gorge of the Waghora river.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Only statements 1 and 2 omit the second phase, which belongs to the Vakataka and Gupta period and the Mahayana sect. Statement 3 is also true, so this combination is incomplete.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Only statements 2 and 3 omit the fact about the 29 caves in Maharashtra. Since statement 1 is also true, leaving it out makes the combination incomplete.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): Only statements 1 and 3 omit the Satavahana-Hinayana first phase, which statement 2 describes correctly. Dropping a true statement makes this combination wrong.

question: The murals of Ajanta mostly depict scenes from
option_1: the life of the Buddha as told in the Jataka stories
solution_text:
The correct answer is the life of the Buddha as told in the Jataka stories.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Ajanta murals mostly depict scenes from the Buddha's life as told in the Jataka stories, making them a visual record of Buddhist narrative (अजंता भित्तिचित्र — जातक कथाएँ)

 

• The paintings of the second phase belong to the Vakataka and Gupta period and show Mahayana influence.

 

• They are done on the walls and ceilings of the rock-cut caves, with natural pigments.

 

• The rich colours, graceful figures and lively detail make them a high point of Indian painting.

 

• Gupta paintings are also associated with other sites, but Ajanta is the best known.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jataka tales narrate the previous births of the Buddha.

 

• The paintings include the Padmapani Bodhisattva.

 

• The caves were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.

 

• Ajanta lies in the Waghora river gorge of Maharashtra, and its Cave 1 holds the famous Bodhisattva Padmapani painting.

 

• The paintings use the fresco-secco method on a prepared plaster of clay and lime.

 

NOTE

 

• the Vedic sacrifices (Option 2): Vedic sacrifices were Brahmanical rituals and not the theme of the Buddhist cave art at Ajanta. The caves were monasteries and prayer halls of Buddhists.

 

• the campaigns of Samudragupta (Option 3): The campaigns of Samudragupta are described in the Allahabad Pillar inscription and not in cave paintings at Ajanta. The murals are religious and not records of conquests.

 

• the life of Mahavira (Option 4): The life of Mahavira is the subject of Jain art, as at Ellora's Jain caves or Udayagiri. Ajanta is a Buddhist site, so it does not show Mahavira's life.

question:
Assertion (A): The Gupta period is called the Golden Age of ancient India.

Reason (R): This period saw remarkable progress in art, science and literature.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion: the Gupta age is called the Golden Age or Classical Age because of its great progress in art, science and literature (गुप्त काल — स्वर्ण युग, कला, विज्ञान और साहित्य की प्रगति)

 

• In literature, the period saw Kalidasa, Visakhadatta, Sudraka and the compilation of the Puranas and the final shaping of the epics.

 

• In science, Aryabhata, Varahamihira and others advanced mathematics, astronomy and medicine.

 

• In art and architecture, temple building, the Ajanta murals and the Bhitargaon temple mark the age.

 

• Political unity and prosperity under strong kings made this cultural flowering possible.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Guptas followed the Kushanas, who were Indo-Scythians.

 

• The Gupta age is also called the Classical Age.

 

• Gold Dinara coins show the prosperity of the empire.

 

• Some historians question the term Golden Age, pointing out that cultural success was centred on courts and cities.

 

• The idea became popular in the early twentieth century, when historians sought a classical age in Indian history.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): This option says R does not explain A, but it does. The cultural advances in art, science and literature are the very reason why the period is considered golden.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): This option says A is true and R is false, but R is true. The notes explicitly state that the period saw remarkable progress in art, science and literature.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): This option says A is false and R true. A is true since the popular name for the Gupta period is the Golden Age, so rejecting it is incorrect.

question: Which of the following pairs of Sanskrit dramas was written by Visakhadatta?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Visakhadatta wrote the Sanskrit dramas Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam, the latter linked with the rise of the Guptas (विशाखदत्त — मुद्राराक्षस और देवीचंद्रगुप्तम्)

 

• Mudrarakshasa is a political play about Chanakya's clever strategy to win over the minister Rakshasa for Chandragupta Maurya.

 

• Devichandraguptam survives only in fragments and helps scholars study how the Guptas came to power.

 

• Visakhadatta's plays are valued for their political themes in contrast to the romantic mood of Kalidasa's dramas.

 

• His works are placed among the main literary sources of the Gupta age.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mrichchakatika was written by Sudraka.

 

• Malavikagnimitram and Vikramorvashiyam are plays of Kalidasa.

 

• Kiratarjuniya by Bharavi is an epic poem about Arjuna and Shiva.

 

• Mudrarakshasa is set in Pataliputra and concerns Chanakya's plan to win over Rakshasa, the former minister of the Nandas.

 

• The play is notable for lacking a heroine, which is unusual in Sanskrit drama.

 

NOTE

 

• Mrichchakatika and Malavikagnimitram (Option 1): Mrichchakatika is a play by Sudraka, and Malavikagnimitram is by Kalidasa. This pair mixes two other authors and contains no work by Visakhadatta.

 

• Vikramorvashiyam and Shakuntalam (Option 2): Vikramorvashiyam and Shakuntalam are both plays by Kalidasa. Neither is by Visakhadatta, so this pair belongs to a different author altogether.

 

• Kiratarjuniya and Mudrarakshasa (Option 4): Kiratarjuniya is an epic by Bharavi on Arjuna's penance and a fight with Shiva, so it is not by Visakhadatta. Though Mudrarakshasa is his, the pair is invalid because of its first member.

question:
Match the works in Column I with their authors in Column II.

Column I: a. Mrichchakatika   b. Panchatantra   c. Amarakosa   d. Shakuntalam

Column II: i. Vishnusharma   ii. Sudraka   iii. Amarasimha   iv. Kalidasa
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct match is Mrichchakatika - Sudraka, Panchatantra - Vishnusharma, Amarakosa - Amarasimha and Shakuntalam - Kalidasa (गुप्तकालीन साहित्य — मृच्छकटिक, पंचतंत्र, अमरकोश, शकुंतलम्)

 

• Sudraka's Mrichchakatika (The Little Clay Cart) is a play full of humour and pathos.

 

• The Panchatantra stories were put together by Vishnusharma in the Gupta period.

 

• Amarasimha, described as a Buddhist author, compiled the lexicon Amarakosa.

 

• Kalidasa, the Shakespeare of India, wrote the drama Shakuntalam.

 

• Kalidasa and Sudraka are usually confused: Kalidasa wrote the epics and romantic plays, while Sudraka's Mrichchakatika is a social drama set in the city of Ujjain.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kalidasa's works include Raghuvamsham, Kumarasambhavam, Meghadutam, Ritusamhara, Vikramorvashiyam and Malavikagnimitram.

 

• Panchatantra was later translated into many languages.

 

• Amarakosa is a Sanskrit thesaurus.

 

• Mrichchakatika portrays the poor Brahmin merchant Charudatta and the courtesan Vasantasena in a story of love and political upheaval.

 

• The Panchatantra was later translated into Pahlavi and Arabic and travelled to Europe.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv (Option 1): This key gives the Mrichchakatika to Vishnusharma and the Panchatantra to Sudraka, reversing the two authors. The clay-cart play is by Sudraka and the fable collection by Vishnusharma.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 3): This key gives the Amarakosa to Kalidasa and Shakuntalam to Amarasimha. The lexicon is by Amarasimha and the drama by Kalidasa, so the last two are interchanged.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv (Option 4): This key gives the Mrichchakatika to Amarasimha and the Amarakosa to Sudraka. The lexicon is the work of Amarasimha and the play the work of Sudraka, so those are interchanged.

question: Which of the following works was NOT composed by Kalidasa?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mrichchakatika.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mrichchakatika is not by Kalidasa; it is a play by Sudraka, full of humour and pathos, while Meghadutam, Ritusamhara and Malavikagnimitram are works of Kalidasa (मृच्छकटिक — शूद्रक की रचना, कालिदास की नहीं)

 

• Kalidasa, called the Shakespeare of India, is credited with seven works: two epics, two lyrics, two plays and the drama Shakuntalam.

 

• His epics are Raghuvamsham and Kumarasambhavam, and his lyrics are Meghadutam and Ritusamhara.

 

• His plays are Vikramorvashiyam and Malavikagnimitram, and the Sanskrit drama is Shakuntalam.

 

• Mrichchakatika is notable for drawing characters from ordinary life including a courtesan and merchant.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kalidasa is associated in tradition with the court of Chandragupta II.

 

• Meghadutam describes a cloud sent as a messenger.

 

• Malavikagnimitram has the Sunga prince Agnimitra as hero.

 

• William Jones's English translation of Shakuntalam in 1789 introduced Kalidasa to the West.

 

• Raghuvamsham traces the line of Raghu, the ancestors of Rama, and Kumarasambhavam tells of the birth of Kartikeya.

 

NOTE

 

• Meghadutam (Option 1): Meghadutam is a lyric poem by Kalidasa in which an exiled Yaksha sends a message through a cloud. Since it is his work, it cannot be the answer to a NOT-type question.

 

• Ritusamhara (Option 2): Ritusamhara is a lyric by Kalidasa describing the six seasons. As the question asks for a work not by him, this correct attribution is eliminated.

 

• Malavikagnimitram (Option 4): Malavikagnimitram is a play by Kalidasa about the Sunga prince Agnimitra and Malavika. It is his work and therefore not the answer to this question.

question:
Consider the following statements about literature in the Gupta period.

1. The Puranas took their present form in this period, and there are eighteen of them.

2. The Bhagavata, Vishnu, Vayu and Matsya are among the most important Puranas.

3. The Mahabharata and the Ramayana were given their final shape in this period.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: the Puranas (18 in number) took their present form, the Bhagavata, Vishnu, Vayu and Matsya are the key ones, and the epics got their final shape in the Gupta age (गुप्तकालीन साहित्य — पुराण, महाभारत, रामायण)

 

• The Puranas deal with creation, genealogies of kings, and religious teachings, and so are also a source of dynastic history.

 

• The Gupta kings' own genealogy is known from the Puranas.

 

• The final redaction of the Mahabharata and Ramayana reflects Brahmanical revival under the Guptas.

 

• Sanskrit became the language of the court and literature, which helped such compilation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Puranas are classed as Mahapuranas and Upapuranas in later tradition.

 

• The Mahabharata's Bhagavad Gita is the most famous section.

 

• Valmiki's Ramayana is called the Adikavya.

 

• The Puranas are traditionally said to have five features: creation, recreation, genealogies, Manu periods and dynastic history.

 

• The Bhagavata Purana's tenth book on Krishna became the base of later bhakti traditions.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Statements 1 and 2 omit the epics, which also reached their final form in this period. Since statement 3 is correct, a combination that leaves it out is incomplete.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): Statements 2 and 3 omit the fact that the Puranas took their present form in this period, with eighteen in number. Statement 1 is true, so leaving it out makes the choice incomplete.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): Statements 1 and 3 omit the list of the key Puranas, which statement 2 gives correctly. Since all three hold, a two-statement combination is incomplete.

question: Which Gupta-period scholar wrote the Aryabhatiya in 499 AD and gave a scientific explanation of solar and lunar eclipses?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Aryabhata.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya in 499 AD, a work on mathematics and astronomy that gives a scientific explanation of solar and lunar eclipses (आर्यभट — आर्यभटीय, 499 ई.)

 

• He is remembered as a great mathematician and astronomer and is credited with the view that the earth rotates on its axis.

 

• His explanation of eclipses replaced the older myth that a demon swallows the sun or moon.

 

• He belongs to the Gupta period, which was a brilliant age for mathematics, astronomy, astrology and medicine.

 

• India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named Aryabhata in his honour.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Aryabhatiya has sections on mathematics, time reckoning and the celestial sphere.

 

• Brahmagupta is a 7th-century astronomer.

 

• Bhaskara II wrote Siddhanta Shiromani in the 12th century.

 

• Aryabhata gave an approximate value of pi as 3.1416, which was quite accurate for his time.

 

• The Aryabhatiya has four sections, including the Ganitapada on mathematics and the Golapada on the celestial sphere.

 

NOTE

 

• Varahamihira (Option 1): Varahamihira composed the Pancha Siddhantika, summarising five astronomical systems, and the Brihat Samhita. He was an astronomer of the Gupta age but did not write the Aryabhatiya.

 

• Brahmagupta (Option 2): Brahmagupta lived in the 7th century and is known for his work on mathematics including rules on zero. He came later than the Gupta period and did not author the Aryabhatiya.

 

• Bhaskara II (Option 4): Bhaskara II wrote the Siddhanta Shiromani in the 12th century. He belongs to the medieval period, centuries after the Gupta age.

question: Which Gupta-age scholar composed the Pancha Siddhantika, which covers five astronomical systems, and the encyclopaedic Brihat Samhita?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Varahamihira.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Varahamihira composed the Pancha Siddhantika on five astronomical systems, the Brihat Samhita and the Brihat Jataka, the standard work on astrology (वराहमिहिर — पंचसिद्धांतिका, बृहत्संहिता)

 

• The Brihat Samhita ranges over astronomy, astrology, geography, architecture, weather, animals, marriage and omens, which makes it an encyclopaedia.

 

• The Brihat Jataka is treated as the standard text on horoscopy.

 

• He is traditionally linked with the court of Chandragupta II as one of its brilliant minds.

 

• His work shows that the Gupta period was a rich age for science.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Varahamihira is also said to have written Laghu Jataka.

 

• The Brihat Samhita is an important work of Sanskrit literature.

 

• Aryabhata and Varahamihira are the two great names of Gupta astronomy.

 

• The Brihat Samhita also includes discussion of rainfall prediction and of vastu, the rules for building temples and houses.

 

• Varahamihira's Brihat Jataka is regarded as the standard text on astrology, while his Pancha Siddhantika summarises older astronomical schools.

 

NOTE

 

• Aryabhata (Option 2): Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya on mathematics and astronomy in 499 AD, which is a different text. He did not write the Pancha Siddhantika or the Brihat Samhita.

 

• Kalidasa (Option 3): Kalidasa was a poet and dramatist who wrote epics, lyrics and plays. He is not an astronomer and did not write on the five astronomical systems.

 

• Charaka (Option 4): Charaka was a physician who wrote the Charaka Samhita on medicine and lived before the Gupta age, according to the notes. He is not the author of any astronomical text.

question:
Consider the following statements about foreign travellers.

1. Fa-Hien, the Chinese pilgrim, visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II.

2. Xuanzang came in the period of Harshavardhana and wrote the Si-yu-ki.

3. Xuanzang visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The travellers' statements about Fa-Hien and Xuanzang hold in this way: Fa-Hien visited during Chandragupta II's reign, and Xuanzang came in Harshavardhana's period and wrote the Si-yu-ki, so statement 3 is wrong (चीनी यात्री — फाह्यान और ह्वेनसांग)

 

• Fa-Hien (Faxian) came for Buddhist texts and left an account of the social, economic and religious life of the Gupta empire.

 

• Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) is called the second Chinese traveller and visited roughly two centuries later in the 7th century.

 

• His Si-yu-ki is a major source for Harsha's reign and for Nalanda.

 

• Confusing the two travellers' periods is a classic SSC error.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Xuanzang studied at Nalanda.

 

• Fa-Hien travelled in the early 5th century.

 

• Yijing was another Chinese traveller of the 7th century.

 

• Fa-Hien's account of his travels is called the Fo-kuo-chi, or Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.

 

• Xuanzang's Si-yu-ki means Records of the Western World, and he travelled in the reign of Harsha in the seventh century.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Statements 2 and 3 together would put Xuanzang in Chandragupta II's time, which is wrong. He lived in the 7th century and wrote of Harsha, so statement 3 cannot be accepted.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Statements 1 and 3 would accept that Xuanzang came in Chandragupta II's reign. That is false, since Fa-Hien visited then and Xuanzang about two centuries later.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): All three cannot be right because statement 3 contradicts the correct statement 2, and it is not possible for Xuanzang to have visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II when he belongs to Harshavardhana's period.

question: On which Gupta ruler's gold coins is the king shown playing the Veena?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Samudragupta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Samudragupta is shown on his coins playing the Veena, a type that fits his title Kaviraja (समुद्रगुप्त — वीणावादक प्रकार के सिक्के)

 

• The Veena-player type reflects his skill in music and poetry, which the Allahabad inscription also praises.

 

• His other famous coin type shows the Ashvamedha horse, recalling his sacrifice after conquests.

 

• Gupta coins carry legends and figures that reveal titles and sacrifices, which makes them a major source.

 

• Together, the coin types show a warrior who was also an artist.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gupta gold coins are called Dinaras.

 

• Samudragupta was a devotee of Vaishnavism.

 

• Chandragupta II issued silver Rupyaka coins.

 

• Gupta gold coins carry Sanskrit legends in Brahmi script, with the king on the obverse and a deity such as Lakshmi on the reverse, which makes them good evidence of royal ideals.

 

• Samudragupta also issued an Archer type showing him with a bow, an image of martial prowess to balance the gentler Veena-player type.

 

• The Veena-player coin legend describes him as Maharajadhiraja, and the reverse shows the goddess Lakshmi.

 

NOTE

 

• Chandragupta II (Option 1): Chandragupta II is known for silver coins and for the Sakari title after defeating the western Sakas. The Veena-player type is not associated with him.

 

• Kumaragupta I (Option 3): Kumaragupta I is known for the peacock and other types linked with his worship of Kartikeya. The Veena type does not belong to him.

 

• Skandagupta (Option 4): Skandagupta's reign was devoted to fighting the Huns, and his coinage did not use the Veena-player type. It belongs to an earlier king.

question: The Gupta dynasty came to power in north India after the decline of which dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Kushanas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Guptas came after the Kushanas, who were Indo-Scythians, and rose to power in north India (गुप्त वंश — कुषाणों के बाद)

 

• The Kushana empire had weakened and broken up, which opened the way for new powers such as the Guptas.

 

• The Mauryas and Sungas were much earlier and the Satavahanas ruled in the Deccan.

 

• The Gupta period is called the Classical Age and the Golden Age of ancient India.

 

• Chandragupta I's marriage with the Lichchhavi princess helped start the rise.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kanishka was the greatest Kushana ruler.

 

• The Gupta Samvat started around 319-320 AD.

 

• Gupta power was built by Chandragupta I and Samudragupta.

 

• The Kushana empire under Kanishka and later kings had declined by the third century AD, which opened a gap in the north.

 

• Several small kingdoms and republics rose after the Kushanas, and the Guptas rose in Magadha.

 

NOTE

 

• The Mauryas (Option 1): The Mauryas ruled from about the fourth century BC to about 185 BC. They were removed by the Sungas centuries before the Guptas, so they were not their immediate predecessors.

 

• The Sungas (Option 2): The Sungas ruled in Magadha after the Mauryas and were succeeded by the Kanvas. They disappeared in the first century BC, long before the rise of the Guptas.

 

• The Satavahanas (Option 4): The Satavahanas ruled in the Deccan and were a southern power. They did not rule the north Indian territory from which the Guptas arose.

question: The Prayaga Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar inscription) of Samudragupta was composed by his court poet
solution_text:
The correct answer is Harisena.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Harisena, the court poet of Samudragupta, composed the Prayaga Prashasti, also called the Allahabad Pillar inscription (हरिषेण — प्रयाग प्रशस्ति के रचयिता)

 

• The prashasti covers how Samudragupta came to the throne, his campaigns in north India and the Deccan, and his gifts as poet and scholar.

 

• Harisena also served the king in high office, which explains his detailed knowledge.

 

• The inscription is a primary source for the Gupta period.

 

• Its Sanskrit, Champu style shows the literary skill of Gupta court poets.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kalidasa belongs to the age of Chandragupta II.

 

• Visakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa.

 

• The pillar originally stood at Kausambi.

 

• Harisena's text is a eulogy, so historians check its claims against coins and other inscriptions to judge their accuracy.

 

• The Allahabad pillar was set up by Ashoka and later carried the Gupta record and a Mughal-period inscription of Jahangir.

 

NOTE

 

• Visakhadatta (Option 1): Visakhadatta was a dramatist who wrote Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam. He was not the court poet who composed the Allahabad inscription.

 

• Sudraka (Option 3): Sudraka wrote the play Mrichchakatika, full of humour and pathos, and is a Gupta-age dramatist, but he had no link with the Allahabad Pillar record or with Samudragupta's court.

 

• Kalidasa (Option 4): Kalidasa wrote epics, lyrics and plays and is linked in tradition with Chandragupta II's court, a later reign. He did not compose Samudragupta's prashasti.
